# Lifecycle functionality (Fallback SDK)

Our SDKs allow indicating when certain milestones in program setup and execution have been reached. If you cannot use the SDK, you can still indicate these milestones by writing [JSONL](https://jsonlines.org/) messages to `$ANTITHESIS_OUTPUT_DIR/sdk.jsonl`.

*Setup* indicates to Antithesis that your system and workload are fully initialized.

To use this functionality, have your program emit the following JSONL once startup is complete:

The item `details` may be any JSON that you wish to log at startup time. If you do not want to record additional information, it may be set to `null` as above. Note that `details` must not terminate with a newline, because the entire message must ultimately be JSONL.

The following *setup* example logs additional information by setting `details`:

*Event* indicates to Antithesis that a certain event has been reached. It provides greater information about the ordering of events during the course of testing in Antithesis. It is a JSONL message consisting of:

- a single top-level field that is the event’s name, which points to
- Arbitrary JSON that contains any details you want to log. Note that these details must not contain any newlines except for the newline that terminates the message. The entire message must ultimately be JSONL.

# Antithesis Assertion Schema

The complete assertions JSON schema is as follows:

    {

      "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-04/schema#",

      "$id": "https://antithesis.com/assertions.schema.json",

      "title": "Antithesis Assertions",

      "description": "This describes the details of an Antithesis assertion",

      "type": "object",

      "properties": {

        "antithesis_assert": {

          "description": "Asserts a specific condition value and reachability",

          "type": "object",

          "properties": {

            "id": {

              "description": "A unique identifier for an assertion",

              "type": "string"

            },

            "message": {

              "description": "Description of the assertion",

              "type": "string"

            },

            "condition": {

              "description": "Evaluation of execution state and location",

              "type": "boolean"

            },

            "display_type": {

              "description": "User-supplied name of the assertion type, for use in reports.",

              "type": "string"

            },

            "hit": {

              "description": "Indicates the assertion was evaluated",

              "type": "boolean"

            },

            "must_hit": {

              "description": "True if the assertion is expected to be evaluated at least once to consider it to be passed",

              "type": "boolean"

            },

            "assert_type": {

              "description": "Type of assertion that was established",

              "type": "string",

              "enum": [

                "always",

                "sometimes",

                "reachability"

              ]

            },

            "location": {

              "description": "Describes physical and logical source code location",

              "type": "object",

              "properties": {

                "file": {

                  "description": "Filename containing the assertion",

                  "type": "string"

                },

                "function": {

                  "description": "Function or method containing the assertion",

                  "type": "string"

                },

                "class": {

                  "description": "Class or package for the code containing the assertion",

                  "type": "string"

                },

                "begin_line": {

                  "description": "Line number for the assertion",

                  "type": "number"

                },

                "begin_column": {

                  "description": "Column number for the assertion",

                  "type": "number"

                }

              }

            },

            "details": {

              "description": "User-provided JSON, for display in reports as additional details. If no additional details are desired, set as null.",

              "type": "object",

              "patternProperties": {

                "^.*$": {

                  "anyOf": [

                    {

                      "type": "string"

                    },

                    {

                      "type": "number"

                    },

                    {

                      "type": "boolean"

                    },

                    {

                      "type": "object"

                    },

                    {

                      "type": "array"

                    },

                    {

                      "type": "null"

                    }

                  ]

                }

              },

              "additionalProperties": false

            }

          }

        }

      }

    }

# Webhooks | Antithesis Docs

Source: https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/webhook/overview/

# Webhooks

You can use webhook calls to initiate the main functions of the platform. The standard webhooks are:

- The `/basic_test endpoint`[test launcher](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/test_launchers/)in the web app.
- The `/debugging endpoint`

All of these webhooks take [parameters](https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/webhook/webhook_reference/) that control the test behavior.

We can also create **custom parameters** for your needs, or advanced users may work with their customer success engineers to build custom endpoints.

Reach out to us at [support@antithesis.com](mailto:support@antithesis.com) to find out more.

# Launching a test | Antithesis Docs

Source: https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/webhook/test_webhook/

# Launching a test

This endpoint kicks off a test using Antithesis’ built-in `Basic_test`. It’s functionally identical to a [test launcher](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/test_launchers/) in the web app.

It first fetches the relevant container images, specified in your configuration files.

Additionally, it also fetches the images specified in `antithesis.images`.

After fetching the images, Antithesis builds the test environment and runs your test for a number of minutes set in `antithesis.duration`.

This webhook returns an HTTP status code to indicate whether it successfully started the test. This code is **not** your test result, it just indicates whether your webhook call worked.

By default, Antithesis orchestrates your containers using docker-compose. To run a test with Kubernetes orchestration instead, use [ /basic_k8s_test](https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/webhook/test_webhook/) instead.

Antithesis webhooks use basic auth credentials for authentication.

The basic auth [machine credentials](https://antithesis.com/docs/configuration/auth) for your tenant.

Your tenant’s name.

The following parameters can be used to configure the webhook. All parameters are optional.

If you want additional ways to parametrize your tests, we can create custom parameters for you, just reach out at [support@antithesis.com](mailto:support@antithesis.com).

These parameters are passed as JSON according to the following template:

###### antithesis.config_image

The image version of your config image. This should be a single image version formatted in the same way as those in the `antithesis.images` parameter.

Examples:

- `"antithesis.config_image": "image_name:latest_tag"`

###### antithesis.description

A description of your test run that’ll be in the headers of the generated report and of any emails triggered by the test run.

###### antithesis.duration

Desired duration of your test run in minutes.

###### antithesis.images

A ;-delimited list of image versions of the software needed in the testing environment. Each entry in the format `[REGISTRY/]NAME(:TAG|@DIGEST)`.

It’s recommended to use a `digest` over a `tag`. Images specified by digest will be tagged as `latest` within [the Antithesis environment](https://antithesis.com/docs/configuration/the_antithesis_environment/).

The default registry will be `us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/molten-verve-216720/$TENANT_NAME-repository/`.

When images mentioned in the config (in `docker-compose.yaml` or in `manifests/`) are also passed via the `antithesis.images` param, the latter overwrites the former. Eg. if your config contains `postgres:17.2` and you pass `docker.io/ubuntu/postgres:17.2` in the param, the image tagged `17.2` will be pulled from the `ubuntu` repository.

We recommend you only use the `antithesis.images` param for passing images not mentioned in the config files.

Examples:

- `"antithesis.images": "registry/container:some_tag"`
- `"antithesis.images": "container_1@sha256:12341234; registry/container_2:latest_tag"`
- `"antithesis.images": "registry/container_1:sha256:12341235; registry/container_2:latest_tag; container_3@sha256:56785678"`

###### antithesis.is_ephemeral

A boolean (represented as `"true"` or `"false"`) that indicates whether or not webhooks’s results should be reflected in future reports as a historic result.

- Set this to `"true"`when kicking-off one-off, exploratory runs. Failing to set this will result in confusing test history.
- Leave this `"false"`(which is the default) when running scheduled tests.

###### antithesis.report.recipients

A ;-delimited list of recipients of emailed links to the triage report produced by this test run.

If this parameter is not specified, emails will be sent to the default users set up for the endpoint.

Examples:

- `"antithesis.report.recipients": "foo@my-site.com"`
- `"antithesis.report.recipients": "u1@site.com; u2@site.com"`

###### antithesis.source

An identifier to separate property history in reports.

In the resulting report, each property’s history is generated from all previous runs with the same `antithesis.source` parameter. This allows you to (for example) easily see the history of tests on a single branch.

The parameter may be arbitrary text, but you will likely provide a source control descriptor.

These parameters allow you to post the results of test runs back to the platform of your choice. In some cases, such as the Antithesis [Github action](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/tooling_integrations/ci/#github-actions), these parameters are automatically configured and you will not need to set them manually.

###### antithesis.integrations.<integration_type>.callback_url

The callback URL.

###### antithesis.integrations.<integration_type>.token

A secret token.

###### <integration_type>

Accepted integration types are `github`, `discord`, and `slack`.

You may post results back to as many different platforms as you like. For example, the following will post results back to both Discord and to Github:

The following parameters are **deprecated**.

###### antithesis.integrations.type

The CI / Source Control integration type.

Values: `["none", "github"]`.

Default value: `"none"`.

###### antithesis.integrations.callback_url

The URL Antithesis will call back to post the test results.

###### antithesis.integrations.token

A security token used to authenticate when calling back with results.

# Launching a debugging session | Antithesis Docs

Source: https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/webhook/notebook_webhook/

# Launching a debugging session

This endpoint kicks off a [multiverse debugging session](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/debugging/advanced_multiverse_debugging/overview/) for a target test run that’ll be available for six hours.

You’ll receive an email with a link to access your session ~5-10 minutes after you call the webhook. If your request is malformed (e.g. an invalid parameter), you’ll receive a non-200 response or a failure email almost immediately.

Once you have the access link, you can start debugging in the [Antithesis Notebook](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/debugging/advanced_multiverse_debugging/antithesis_notebook/).

The target test run is identified by `antithesis.debugging.run_id`. For backwards compatibility, `antithesis.debugging.session_id` is also accepted but prefer `run_id` for new integrations.

Antithesis webhooks use basic auth credentials for authentication.

The basic auth [machine credentials](https://antithesis.com/docs/configuration/auth) for your tenant.

Your tenant’s name.

These parameters are passed as JSON according to the following template:

You can request a debugging session using either `antithesis.debugging.run_id` or `antithesis.debugging.session_id`. Although they are not marked as required below, you must provide either one of them in your request.

###### antithesis.debugging.input_hash

###### antithesis.debugging.run_id

Run ID of the test run you want to start debugging. Obtain it from the runs view by copying from the ⋮ menu of the run, or by copying it from the bottom of the triage report.

Although this parameter is not marked as required, you need to provide either the run ID or the session ID of the test run to debug in the request. Prefer `run_id` over `session_id` for new integrations.

###### antithesis.debugging.session_id

Session ID of the test run you want to start debugging. Obtain it from the [copy moment](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/reports/properties/#copy-moment) button in the triage report.

Although this parameter is not marked as required, you need to provide either the run ID or the session ID of the test run to debug in the request. Prefer `run_id` over `session_id` for new integrations.

###### antithesis.debugging.vtime

###### antithesis.report.recipients

A `;`-delimited list of recipients who’ll receive emailed links to the triage report produced by this test run.

If this parameter is not specified, emails will be sent to the default users set up for the endpoint.

Examples:

- `"antithesis.report.recipients": "u1@site.com; u2@site.com"`

# Handling external dependencies | Antithesis Docs

Source: https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/dependencies/

# Handling external dependencies

This is a detailed discussion of how to handle your system’s dependencies for testing in Antithesis. Remember, testing happens in a hermetic testing environment with no internet access, because your software’s always wanted its own little Faraday cage.

For an overview of this topic, please read the [Docker Setup guide](https://antithesis.com/docs/getting_started/setup_guide/docker_compose/#containerize-your-dependencies) or the [Kubernetes Setup guide](https://antithesis.com/docs/getting_started/setup_guide/setup_k8s/#dependencies).

Each of your software’s dependencies can be provided either as:

- An actual, containerized service, just like you’d use in production.
- A mock of the service, which could be pre-built (e.g., Localstack), or something you write yourself. You’ll use this approach for external dependencies that can’t be containerized (e.g. AWS S3), or when the service provider hasn’t made docker images available.

This directory lists containerized open-source services and prebuilt mocks. You can include them in a [Docker Compose file](https://antithesis.com#docker-code-for-including-dependencies), or add the [Kubernetes manifests](https://antithesis.com#kubernetes-manifests-for-dependencies) for them.

If you’d like something added to this directory please let us know at [support@antithesis.com](mailto:support@antithesis.com).

Antithesis has been extensively tested with both [Localstack](https://www.localstack.cloud/) and [MinIO](https://min.io/). As of June 2025, we recommend using MinIO in place of S3 when you test in Antithesis, and mocking all other AWS services with Localstack, mostly because the free version of Localstack does not persist data to disk, which many customers require. We provide [sample  docker-compose.yaml blocks](https://antithesis.com#localstack) for both of these below.

Localstack supports many services, including:

- DynamoDB
- S3
- Lambda
- CloudWatch
- SSM
- IAM
- SQS

Other pre-built mocks for AWS include:

Any open source dependencies available on [Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com/) or any public registry can simply be uploaded to Antithesis along with your software. Here are some commonly used ones, If you’d like something added to this directory please let us know at [support@antithesis.com](mailto:support@antithesis.com).

- [Aerospike](https://hub.docker.com/_/aerospike)
- [Cassandra](https://hub.docker.com/_/cassandra)
- [Clickhouse](https://hub.docker.com/_/clickhouse)
- [Cockroach](https://hub.docker.com/r/cockroachdb/cockroach)
- [CouchDB](https://hub.docker.com/_/couchdb)
- [ElasticSearch](https://hub.docker.com/_/elasticsearch)
- [Grafana-loki](https://hub.docker.com/r/grafana/loki)
- [Grafana-mimir](https://hub.docker.com/r/grafana/mimir)
- [InfluxDB](https://hub.docker.com/_/influxdb)
- [Jaeger](https://hub.docker.com/r/jaegertracing/jaeger)
- [MariaDB](https://hub.docker.com/_/mariadb)
- [Memcached](https://hub.docker.com/_/memcached)
- [MongoDB](https://hub.docker.com/r/bitnami/mongodb)
- [MySQL](https://hub.docker.com/_/mysql)

# Product FAQs | Antithesis Docs

Source: https://antithesis.com/docs/faq/customer_faq/

# Product FAQs

##  #### Can I use an AI agent to help me with setup?

  ##  #### Troubleshooting common setup pitfalls

 | Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Test run fails with a build error. | Incorrect container image architecture. | Build container images for x86-64 CPUs: `docker build --platform linux/amd64`. |
| Generic network connection errors. | Antithesis runs your software in a hermetic testing environment with no internet access. | Bake all dependencies into Docker images at build time or [mock them](https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/dependencies/). |
| Fault injection starts at unexpected points, e.g. during system initialization. | Antithesis expects exactly one `setup_complete`signal from the system. | Check if your system is emitting `setup_complete`from multiple containers or multiple scripts. |
| Test artifacts don’t include logs you expect. | Antithesis relies on the default logging driver to capture logs from all containers. A custom logging driver in `docker-compose.yaml`will cause your logs to be filtered out. | Remove any logging driver configs and use the default. |

##  #### How should I think about testing with Antithesis?

 To use Antithesis effectively, you need to stop thinking about testing in **imperative** terms and think in **declarative** terms. Instead of asking “what sequence of events will cause a failure?”, ask “what must always be true, no matter what happens?”.

| Traditional testing | Antithesis testing | |
|---|---|---|
| Test structure | Imperative: step A, then B, then assert C. | Declarative: define properties that must always/sometimes hold. |
| Fault injection | You script specific failures. | Antithesis injects faults autonomously and you don’t control when or what. |
| How tests run | Tests are run outside the system where they observe and make assertions. | Tests are clients and run alongside the system, in the same environment. |
| Reproducibility | Flaky tests are common. | Every failure is reproducible via deterministic replay. |

Imagine you’re testing a message queue. When writing an integration or end-to-end test you would:

But when testing with Antithesis, you would define:

You don’t script any failure scenarios. Antithesis subjects your system to a wide variety of failure scenarios for you: it kills brokers, partitions the network, and pauses processes on its own.

Your job is to:

- define correct system behavior
- give Antithesis access to as much of the code surface as you can

##  #### How do I iterate locally and for Antithesis in the same docker-compose.yaml file?

 Antithesis expects to receive pre-built images for your containers defined in the `docker-compose.yaml` file. But, this doesn’t mean you have to use two different `docker-compose.yaml` files, one for local iteration and one for Antithesis.

You can use [compose build](https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/build/) to build images for local iteration, and define pre-built images for Antithesis to pull.

Here’s an example:

`${REPOSITORY}` is an environment variable injected via a .env file. You must set this variable for the above to work.

When iterating locally, to bring up your system, run:

This rebuilds containers which have a `build` attribute and tags them as `latest`.

When Antithesis attempts to bring up your system, it’ll use the pre-built images by resolving the `REPOSITORY` and `IMAGES_TAG` env variables you define in a .env file. If you don’t set `IMAGES_TAG`, it defaults to `latest`.

##  #### How do I validate my setup?

 You can manually validate your setup by disconnecting from the internet, running `docker-compose up` locally and verifying that all services are running as expected. If this happens, you should be able to call the [ basic_test](https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/webhook/test_webhook/) webhook successfully.

To streamline this process, you can automate it using a GitHub Action. The [example workflow](https://github.com/antithesishq/etcd-test-composer/blob/gh-action-docker-compose-up/.github/workflows/build-push-validate-test.yml) includes steps to build the project, validate the local setup, run and validate test commands, and finally call the [ basic_test](https://antithesis.com/docs/reference/webhook/test_webhook/) endpoint.

We recommend setting up either this or a similar workflow in your CI pipeline.

##  #### How do I validate test commands locally?

 To validate your test commands locally:

- Run `docker-compose up`, without internet connection, to bring up your system.
- Run the individual test commands using `docker exec <CONTAINER_NAME> path/to/test-file/`.`<CONTAINER_NAME>`is the container containing the test command.

If the test commands run successfully then you’re good to kick off an actual test. [This page](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/test_templates/testing_locally/) has more details.

##  #### How often should we test?

 Most Antithesis customers run tests nightly to catch bugs and regressions as early in development as possible, and some also run shorter tests on every commit to help reduce the feedback cycle for active development.

-
Nightly tests: - Run for 6-8hrs.
- Uncover bugs that are hard to find. The longer a test runs, the more states are explored.

-
Short tests: - Run on a commit to the main development branch.
- Run for ~30min - 1hr.
- Catch simple bugs that slipped through conventional unit and end-to-end tests.

##  #### What are “test hours” and how are they measured?

 “Test hours” refers to the total time the System Under Test (SUT) experiences across an entire test run.

It’s roughly equivalent to the total active CPU time during the run, and can be estimated as:
`antithesis.duration × number of CPU cores provisioned`.

##  #### Is there a way to bias test runs? If I believe there's a bug in subsystem X can I get Antithesis to apply more effort to a subset of our tests?

 Yes, there are several ways to focus on a particular subsystem:

- Write more [test drivers](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/test_templates/test_composer_reference/#test-commands)that call the subsystem.
- Put more [assertions](https://antithesis.com/docs/concepts/properties_assertions/assertions/)in the subsystem or the clients that exercise the subsystem.
- Talk to our customer success engineers to help tune the configuration: [support@antithesis.com](mailto:support@antithesis.com).

##  #### Which S3 mocks do you support?

  ##  #### Is there a logging limit in Antithesis? Can I run my system with full debugging logs?

 Best practice when testing with Antithesis is to use a moderate amount of logging — remember that the platform’s determinism makes it easy to reproduce and replay any bug you find, and with [multiverse debugging](https://antithesis.com/docs/product/debugging/advanced_multiverse_debugging/overview/) you can turn full debugging logs on at any point during the replay.

For each simulation hour within the Antithesis environment, Antithesis will provide two hundred (200) megabytes of searchable log storage and container image storage for a customer for six (6) months.

If your system exceeds the 200 MB/test hour limit, the output/logging limit property in your report will fail. [This section](https://antithesis.com/docs/best_practices/optimizing/#avoid-excessive-logging-output) has details on how to do this.

Can you run with full DEBUG logs? Well, it depends on:

- How verbose your DEBUG logs are.
- How many services are logging at DEBUG level.
- Where the logs are written (e.g., DEBUG to disk, INFO to stdout is preferable).
- The overall scale of your system.

In general, smaller-scale systems with flexible logging setups are more likely to stay within the limit.

##  #### What are some common uses of sometimes assertions?

 [Sometimes assertions](https://antithesis.com/docs/concepts/properties_assertions/sometimes_assertions/) are important signposts along the software execution paths that can be useful in many ways.

-
Making rare bugs more common: If you encounter a bug infrequently and you want to reproduce it with more logging, you should add a sometimes assertion in the relevant parts of code. Or if you’ve tackled a flaky issue and want to make sure it’s actually fixed, sometimes assertions help Antithesis hit those code blocks more often.
-
Hit more edge cases in a test: It’s useful to write sometimes assertions for known edge cases that you want to test, so you know that the test actually ran your edge case. If it doesn’t pass, maybe you’re either not running the simulation long enough or you need to strengthen your test template to hit this scenario. For example, if you’re writing a search algorithm, maybe you add a sometimes assertion to ensure that Antithesis has encountered scenarios where the item is at the end of the list.
-
Ensure the system is being exercised: Make sure that minimum amount of work is being done during each test. Adding simple and intuitive sometimes assertions of some work being done in the system provides assurance that your system was correctly exercised. For example, if your product is a database, maybe you add a sometimes assertion to ensure Antithesis has encountered scenarios where a table has more than 1000 rows.

# About Antithesis POCs | Antithesis Docs

Source: https://antithesis.com/docs/faq/poc_faq/

# About Antithesis POCs

The goal of our POCs is to prove that Antithesis can help you find and fix the bugs that give you nightmares — the kind that cause outages and correctness issues and tie up your best engineers for weeks.

We structure them to require minimal effort from your team, and we want to be up front about who’ll need to be involved on your side to make this maximally informative and effective for you.

[Contact us](https://antithesis.com/company/contact/?topic=book-a-demo) to book a demo.

No!

Antithesis will strengthen almost any testing regime, by verifying correctness and availability under really strenuous conditions.

[Many customers](https://antithesis.com/) already trust Antithesis to improve software reliability and boost engineering velocity.

Our POCs are 2-week sprints.

We’ll work with your team to find, debug and regression test a known bug that your team had a hard time solving in the past — what we call a “brown M&M.” This will give you an accurate picture of what it’s like to use Antithesis, and how much we can boost your development velocity.

Most companies that engage in a POC not only find their known bug, but discover other, previously unknown issues in their software as well.

Two weeks, two phases, no complications.

Most of this can be completed ahead of time.

- Before we start, pick a known bug to look for. See [What kind of known bug should we use?](https://antithesis.com#what-kind-of-known-bug-should-we-use)below.
- At or before kick off, provide a [containerized build](https://antithesis.com/docs/getting_started/setup_guide/docker_compose/#containerize-your-software)of your system that includes your known bug.
- Lift-and-shift one or more of your integration tests or end-to-end (e2e) tests into Antithesis.
- Start testing!

- Start testing in Antithesis.
- Iterate on your testing until we find the bug (and probably some other issues as well).
- Use our advanced debugging tools to triage and debug.
- Upload a new version of the software with your fix.
- Re-test the new build to confirm your fix has worked.

You should make sure you have the right team lined up to make this happen. If this expertise already resides within your team, or if you can be assured of this support, you’re off to a great start.

| Expertise needed | What’s needed from them |
|---|---|
| Build, run, deploy | A lot of the setup work will fall on the build team; securing their bandwidth is crucial. Overall, you should plan 2-4 days of developer time depending on your system. |
| Cybersecurity | Provision SSO, check policies. You’ll likely need no more than a few hours from 1 person, but it’s essential. |
| Knowledge of the SUT (this is typically your team’s SWEs) | Design and iterate on testing. Triage test results and fix bugs discovered. You’ll need 1-2 dev-days to do the initial test, but then you can invest more time in triaging, fixing, and iterating. |
| Dependency owners | If your system has dependencies owned by other teams at the company, you’ll likely need their help. If they have pre-built mocks for their APIs (and they should!), they’ll just be doing basic support. |

The best place to look is your production bug tracker. Pick the worst, hardest-to-find, hardest-to-debug issue you can find. The more miserable it made you, the better it works as a “brown M&M”.

The bug you pick should have several of the following qualities:

- Finding the issue took a long time, because:
- The root cause was very far from the symptom, or
- It showed up very rarely in production.

- Reproducing/triaging the issue was difficult, because:
- It relied on specific timings that were hard to reproduce, or
- There were multiple potential causes.

- The issue re-appeared after being “fixed.”
- A clear indicator of the issue exists, such as a unique log line.

General classes of issue that tend to meet these criteria are:

- Race conditions
- Concurrency issues
- Execution timing issues
- Data corruption issues

Van Halen was notorious for requiring concert venues to sign a lengthy contract before they’d agree to play. The contract defined precise technical specifications vital to the safety of the band’s pyrotechnics-laden shows. Buried within it was a line specifying a bowl of M&M candies in the dressing room *with all of the brown ones removed.*

The “no brown M&Ms” clause was a quick test of whether the venue had actually read the contract carefully. A glance at the bowl of candy immediately told the band whether they needed to take a thorough look at the rest of the setup as well.

We’re not trying to stage a rock concert, but we believe this is a great, low-effort way to establish whether Antithesis will help you resolve bugs that you’ve previously found difficult or time-consuming to resolve.

# A distributed systems reliability glossary | Antithesis Docs

Source: https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/

# A distributed systems reliability glossary

This glossary is an overview of the concepts that you’ll need to think about distributed systems reliability. We’re writing chiefly for industry practitioners – software developers who are learning about distributed systems testing at any stage of their careers.

It’s meant as a handy guide, bringing together information that was previously scattered all over the internet — because the concepts here originate in many different disciplines (and naturally everyone’s too shy to talk to people outside their field, us included). To the best of our knowledge, it’s the first resource to do so. At the same time, we hope that simply putting all these ideas together in one place starts to show how they all fit together.

But! And we cannot stress this enough — **this is a reference, not required reading!**

We’re not saying you need to understand every one of these concepts in order to test a distributed system. Every time you write an integration test, you’re testing a distributed system already! This glossary is here to encourage you to get deeper into a topic that’s increasingly important for every developer committing production code today.

So our goal is to provide intuitive explanations, with pointers to more formal definitions should you need them. We present clear, univalent definitions of terms that are actually messy and contested, like “process,” “repeatable read” or “eventual consistency.” In such cases, we attempt to nod at the diversity of definitions and usages that exists, but our priority is to give a reader something that’s directionally correct and actually useful for a learner.

We’ve also included essential concepts for which there are no formally defined or widely accepted terms in existing literature, like “[garbage reads](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/#garbage-read)” and “[g-nonadjacent](https://antithesis.com#g-nonadjacent-non-adjacent-anti-dependency-cycle).” Maybe the names will stick?

We know it’s incomplete, and if you care about software reliability or distributed systems, [we’d love your help](mailto:bugbash@antithesis.com?subject=Contributing to the Reliability Glossary)!

This glossary is organized as follows:

- [Preliminaries](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/#preliminaries):- [phenomena](https://antithesis.com#phenomena)and- [consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models).
- [Consistency models](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/#consistency-models):
- [Availability models](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/#availability-models):
- [Phenomena](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/#phenomena):
- [Faults](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/#faults):
- [Testing techniques](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/#testing-techniques):
- [Further reading](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/reliability_glossary/#further-reading):

Regardless of whether you’re working on your first distributed system or your fiftieth, we hope this will help you make it more reliable.

Yours, [Jepsen](https://jepsen.io/) & [Antithesis](https://antithesis.com/)

These concepts are used often in defining [phenomena](https://antithesis.com#phenomena) and [consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models).

- [Dependency](https://antithesis.com#dependency)
- In [consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models), a[dependency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies)is a relationship between two[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)(e.g. transactions). For example, a single[process](https://antithesis.com#process)could execute one operation before another: a[process dependency](https://antithesis.com#process-dependency). One operation could read data that was written by another: a[write-read dependency](https://antithesis.com#write-read-dependency).
- [Definite error](https://antithesis.com#definite-error)
- A definite error is returned by an [operation](https://antithesis.com#operation)which definitely did not happen. For instance, a transaction abort error is usually a definite error: the state of the system should be as if the transaction never happened at all. By contrast, an[indefinite error](https://antithesis.com#indefinite-error)may mean that the requested operation did or did not happen, or might happen later.
- [Indefinite error](https://antithesis.com#indefinite-error)
- An indefinite error is returned by an [operation](https://antithesis.com#operation)which may or may not have happened, or might happen later. For instance, a timeout is an indefinite error: the operation may not have been received at all, or it may have taken place without an acknowledgement, or it may be in-flight and execute five minutes later. By contrast, a[definite error](https://antithesis.com#definite-error)is known to have not executed.
 Distinguishing between definite and indefinite errors is a key challenge in distributed systems design and testing. If one writes a unique value x = 3, receives a definite error, and later reads x = 3, that very likely signals an invariant violation. If the write receives an indefinite error, it is legal to read x = 3 now, at some later time, or never at all. Checkers must account for all possible outcomes.
- [Object](https://antithesis.com#object)
- In consistency models, a database usually contains a set of distinct *objects*, also called*items*. Each object often has a unique identifier, and over time, goes through a series of*versions*
- [Operation](https://antithesis.com#operation)
- Operations are “the things a system does.” Exactly what constitutes an operation depends on the system or formalism.
 For instance, the operations performed by a queuing system might be “enqueue” and “dequeue.” A counter system might have “increment” and “read.” A user-registration system might have operations like “register a user,” “log in,” and “change password.” Systems can also have other kinds of operations. For example, a test of a database system might define an operation for “compact old files,” or “add a node to the cluster.” Similarly,[faults](https://antithesis.com#faults)can be viewed as operations: “kill a[process](https://antithesis.com#process)” or “[partition the network](https://antithesis.com#network-partition)” are things one can do to a system.
 Transaction systems can be interpreted a few ways. Much of the[transaction consistency literature](https://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/adya-phd.pdf)uses the term “operation” to refer to (e.g.) an individual read or write of some[object](https://antithesis.com#object). These small operations are then grouped into transactions. On the other hand, it can also be convenient to think of a transaction as a single operation; this makes symmetries between single-object consistency models like[Linearizability](https://antithesis.com#linearizability)and multi-object models like[Serializability](https://antithesis.com#serializability)clearer.
- [Predicate](https://antithesis.com#predicate)
- A *predicate*[objects](https://antithesis.com#object), rather than identifying a single object by primary key. For example “every box containing a cat” is a predicate; so is “all boxes.” A system may offer different levels of safety for[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)which access individual items, vs. operations which use a predicate.
- [Process](https://antithesis.com#process)
- For our purposes, a *process*(which depending on context, may also be called an agent, actor, node, machine, replica, server, session, etc.) is a logically single-threaded state machine which participates in a distributed system.
 We can often interpret a single database client as a process. However, once a client requests an[operation](https://antithesis.com#operation)which results in an indefinite error, it can perform no further operations — that operation might take place at some later time. Were it to perform another operation, it might execute the two concurrently, and no longer be “logically single-threaded.”
- [Process dependency](https://antithesis.com#process-dependency)
- A [process dependency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies#process)relates two subsequent[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)performed by the same process. If process P performs operation A, then B, we say that B process-depends on A.
 It can be convenient to identify a session as a single process and vice-versa (making[session dependencies](https://antithesis.com#session-dependency)process dependencies), but a single process could execute more than one session, and a session could in some systems be handed off between two processes (thereby making it useful to distinguish the two types of dependency).
- [Real-time dependency](https://antithesis.com#real-time-dependency)
- A [real-time dependency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies#real-time)relates two[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)which were not concurrent in real time. If operation A ends before operation B begins, B real-time-depends on A. Real-time dependencies are useful for finding violations of real-time[consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models)like[Strong Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable).
- [Read-write dependency](https://antithesis.com#read-write-dependency)
- A [read-write dependency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies#read-write)relates two operations A and B, where A reads some[version](https://antithesis.com#version)v1 of an[object](https://antithesis.com#object)x, and B writes the next version v2 of x. Speaking loosely, we can say A did not see some part of B, and therefore must have executed before it. Read-write dependencies are used to define stronger[consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models)like[Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read),[Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation), and[Serializability](https://antithesis.com#serializability).
- [Session dependency](https://antithesis.com#session-dependency)
- Some systems provide a notion of a *session*: a sequence of[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)performed in total order, usually by a single client or[process](https://antithesis.com#process). A[session dependency](https://software.imdea.org/~gotsman/papers/si-podc16.pdf)relates two operations performed within a session: if the session performs operation A, then B, we say that B session-depends on A. Session dependencies can be used to define session[consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models)like[Strong Session Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-session-serializable).
 A single process could execute more than one session, and a session could (in some systems) be handed off between two processes. A test harness might choose to view each session as a single process; in this case, session dependencies and process dependencies are equivalent.
- [Version](https://antithesis.com#version)
- In [consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models), a[version](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies#preliminaries)refers to a specific state that some[object](https://antithesis.com#object)took on. Formalisms differ, but in broad terms, every write of an object generally produces a new version of that object, and every read generally returns one (or more) versions. Two different versions may have the same value: if one operation sets x = 3, and another also sets x = 3, those are two different versions of x.
- [Version order](https://antithesis.com#version-order)
- A [version order](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies#preliminaries)is an order over versions of objects in a database, which encodes the sequence of versions each object took on during some execution. In[Adya’s formalism](https://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/icde00.pdf), the version order is total over the versions of any single object.
- [Write-read dependency](https://antithesis.com#write-read-dependency)
- A [write-read dependency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies#write-read)relates two[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)A and B, where A writes some[version](https://antithesis.com#version)v1 of an object x, and B reads v1. Speaking loosely, B observes A’s write. Write-read dependencies help trace the way information flows between operations, and are used to define[consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models)like[Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed).
- [Write-write dependency](https://antithesis.com#write-write-dependency)
- A [write-write dependency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies#write-write)relates two[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)A and B, where A writes some[version](https://antithesis.com#version)v1 of an[object](https://antithesis.com#object)x, and B writes v2: the next version of x in the version order. Speaking informally, B overwrites A’s write. Write-write dependencies help trace the way information flows between operations, and are used to define[consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models)like[Read Uncommitted](https://antithesis.com#read-uncommitted).

These properties define what systems are allowed to do. Each consistency model usually proscribes some set of phenomena.

We draw many of our definitions of consistency models and phenomena from papers like Berenson et al’s [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf), Adya’s 1999 thesis [Weak Consistency](http://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/adya-phd.pdf), and Cerone et al’s [A Framework for Transactional Consistency Models with Atomic Visibility](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol042-concur2015/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2015.58/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2015.58.pdf). In a broad sense, this line of research is an attempt to fix the incomplete and ambiguous definitions in the [ANSI SQL standard](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/23/cncpt/data-concurrency-and-consistency.html#GUID-7F2C6927-5482-4144-B43B-5E90EF4E055B). Other models and phenomena are adapted from Fekete et al’s [Making Snapshot Isolation Serializable](https://dsf.berkeley.edu/cs286/papers/ssi-tods2005.pdf), Cerone & Gotsman’s [Analyzing Snapshot Isolation](https://dsf.berkeley.edu/cs286/papers/ssi-tods2005.pdf), Bailis et al’s [Highly Available Transactions](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol7/p181-bailis.pdf) and [Scalable Atomic Visibility with RAMP Transactions](http://www.bailis.org/papers/ramp-sigmod2014.pdf), and so on.

- [Consistency model](https://antithesis.com#consistency-model)
- A [consistency model](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models)is a set of allowed histories. It constrains which[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)are permissible, and in which orders. We say that one model is stronger than another if the stronger model’s allowed histories are a strict subset of the weaker model’s allowed histories.
 For example,[Monotonic Read](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-reads)is a consistency model which requires that for each[process](https://antithesis.com#process), reads never “go backwards.”[Serializability](https://antithesis.com#serializability)is a consistency model which requires that the outcomes of[operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)are equivalent to if those operations had been executed in total order.
- [Causal consistency](https://antithesis.com#causal-consistency)
- [Causal consistency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/causal)ensures that when a single- [process](https://antithesis.com#process)(sometimes called a “node” or “session”) performs a series of- [operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)on an object, other processes observe those operations in the same order. A variant of causal consistency, Real Time Causal, is one of the strongest totally available consistency models.
- [Eventual consistency](https://antithesis.com#eventual-consistency)
- [Eventual consisistency](https://inria.hal.science/hal-00932836/file/CRDTs_SSS-2011.pdf)requires that after updates cease, given sufficient time and network messages, every node reaches the same final value. Eventually consistent systems provide- [total availability](https://antithesis.com#total-availability): reads and updates can always be performed locally, without network communication.
- [History](https://antithesis.com#history)
- Speaking loosely, a history is a set of [operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)performed by some system, along with information like “what[process](https://antithesis.com#process)performed each operation” and “when did each operation begin and end. A history is often concurrent: at any given time, several operations may be executed by different processes.
 Conceptually, a[consistency model](https://antithesis.com#consistency-model)is[a set of allowable histories](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol042-concur2015/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2015.58/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2015.58.pdf). In practice, distributed systems tests often record a history, then try to determine whether it satisfied some properties. To do this, the test may[establish a mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.10554)between the recorded history as seen by the test harness, and the abstract history used to define some consistency model.
- [Linearizability](https://antithesis.com#linearizability)
- [Linearizability](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/linearizable)is a consistency model which ensures that on a single- [object](https://antithesis.com#object),- [operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)appear to execute atomically (i.e. not interleaved with other operations), in a total order, and that order is consistent with the real-time order of operations. If operation A ends before operation B begins, A must appear to execute before B. This holds regardless of which process performs an operation.
 Relaxing Linearizability’s real-time constraint gives- [Sequential Consistency](https://antithesis.com#sequential-consistency-model). If one identifies a transaction as an operation, and the entire database as a single object, Linearizability is equivalent to- [Strong Serializability](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable).
- [Monotonic Atomic View](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-atomic-view)
- [Monotonic Atomic View](https://amplab.cs.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2013/10/hat-vldb2014.pdf)is a less-common, totally- [available](https://antithesis.com#availability-models)transactional consistency model. It strengthens- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed)by requiring that: once a transaction T1 observes any effect of some other transaction T2, T2 must observe all effects of T1. This is particularly helpful for preventing missing foreign keys, or for ensuring indices and materialized views don’t miss their underlying objects.
 Monotonic Atomic View is weaker than- [Read Atomic](https://antithesis.com#read-atomic),- [Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read), and- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation).
- [Monotonic Reads](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-reads)
- [Monotonic Reads](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/monotonic-reads)is a consistency model which guarantees that each- [process](https://antithesis.com#process)observes a monotonically advancing view of the system. Once a process observes the effects of some write, it must always observe those effects.
- [Monotonic Writes](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-writes)
- [Monotonic Writes](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/monotonic-writes)is a consistency model which guarantees that if a single- [process](https://antithesis.com#process)performs two writes, all processes observe those two writes in that order. The second write should “overwrite” the first.
- [Read Atomic](https://antithesis.com#read-atomic)
- [Read Atomic](http://www.bailis.org/papers/ramp-sigmod2014.pdf)is a transactional consistency model which ensures atomic visibility: either all or none of a transaction’s updates are observed by other transactions. Read Atomic prevents- [Fractured Read](https://antithesis.com#fractured-read),- [Aborted Read](https://antithesis.com#g1a-aborted-read), and- [Intermediate Read](https://antithesis.com#g1b-intermediate-read); it is stronger than- [Monotonic Atomic View](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-atomic-view)in that it prevents Fractured Read. Read Atomic is weaker than- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation).
- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed)
- [Read Committed](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/read-committed)is a relatively weak transactional consistency model which strengthens- [Read Uncommitted](https://antithesis.com#read-uncommitted). It proscribes- [Write Cycle](https://antithesis.com#g0-write-cycle),- [Aborted Read](https://antithesis.com#g1a-aborted-read),- [Intermediate Read](https://antithesis.com#g1b-intermediate-read), and- [Cyclic Information Flow](https://antithesis.com#g1c-cyclic-information-flow). However, it allows all forms of- [Anti-Dependency Cycle](https://antithesis.com#g2-anti-dependency-cycle): cycles where one transaction fails to observe another’s effects. Read Committed can be- [totally available](https://antithesis.com#total-availability).
 Read Committed strengthens- [Read Uncommitted](https://antithesis.com#read-uncommitted)by proscribing Aborted Read, Intermediate Read, and Cyclic Information Flow. It is weaker than- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation)(which proscribes- [Non-Adjacent Anti-Dependency Cycle](https://antithesis.com#g-nonadjacent-non-adjacent-anti-dependency-cycle)) and- [Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read)(which proscribes Anti-Dependency Cycle).
- [Read Uncommitted](https://antithesis.com#read-uncommitted)
- [Read Uncommitted](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/read-uncommitted)is one of the weakest transactional consistency models. Definitions vary, but in- [Adya’s formalism](https://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/icde00.pdf), Read Uncommitted proscribes- [G0](https://antithesis.com#g0-write-cycle): transactions should not overwrite each other’s effects. However, Read Uncommitted allows- [G1](https://antithesis.com#g1), and more. Read Uncommitted can be- [totally available](https://antithesis.com#total-availability).
 Read Uncommitted is weaker than- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed), which, in addition to G0, proscribes G1.
- [Read Your Writes](https://antithesis.com#read-your-writes)
- [Read Your Writes](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/read-your-writes)is a consistency model which ensures that if a- [process](https://antithesis.com#process)performs a write, any subsequent read performed by that same process must observe that write’s effects.
- [Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read)
- [Repeatable Read](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/repeatable-read)is a transactional consistency model which strengthens- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed). It proscribes- [G0](https://antithesis.com#g0-write-cycle),- [G1](https://antithesis.com#g1), and- [G2-item](https://antithesis.com#g2-item-item-anti-dependency-cycle): cycles between transactions which fail to observe each other’s effects, based on single-- [object](https://antithesis.com#object)reads.
 Repeatable Read is stronger than Read Committed, which allows- [G2-item](https://antithesis.com#g2-item-item-anti-dependency-cycle). It is weaker than- [Serializability](https://antithesis.com#serializability), which proscribes- [G2](https://antithesis.com#g2-anti-dependency-cycle)in general, not just on single-item reads. It follows that Repeatable Read and Serializable are indistinguishable from Serializable for transactions which interact with objects by primary key; they differ only with respect to predicate- [phenomena](https://antithesis.com#phenomena).
 Definitions and implementations of Repeatable Read vary widely. We use- [Adya’s PL-2.99](https://www.pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/adya-phd.pdf), which is often used in research on consistency models. The ANSI SQL specification offers a- [much weaker, ambiguous definition](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf)which, unlike PL-2.99, allows- [G0](https://antithesis.com#g0-write-cycle)(write cycle).
- [Serializability](https://antithesis.com#serializability)
- [Serializability](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/serializable)is a relatively strong transactional consistency model which requires that all transactions appear to execute in some total order. It is stronger than- [Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read)and- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation), proscribing- [G0](https://antithesis.com#g0-write-cycle),- [G1](https://antithesis.com#g1), and- [G2](https://antithesis.com#g2-anti-dependency-cycle). It does not require that the apparent order of transactions be consistent with the per-- [process](https://antithesis.com#process)or real-time order: for that, see- [Strong Session Serializability](https://antithesis.com#strong-session-serializable)and- [Strong Serializability](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable), respectively.
- [Sequential (consistency model)](https://antithesis.com#sequential-consistency-model)
- [Sequential](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models)consistency is a relatively strong consistency model which guarantees that all- [operations](https://antithesis.com#operation)appear to take place in some total order, and that order is consistent with the order on each- [process](https://antithesis.com#process). Sequential is stronger than- [Causal](https://antithesis.com#causal-consistency), in that it requires equivalence to a total order of operations. It is weaker than- [Linearizable](https://antithesis.com#linearizability), in that it does not require real-time order.
- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation)
- [Snapshot Isolation](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/snapshot-isolation)is a transactional consistency model which strengthens- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed). It proscribes- [G0](https://antithesis.com#g0-write-cycle),- [G1](https://antithesis.com#g1), and- [G-nonadjacent](https://antithesis.com#g-nonadjacent-non-adjacent-anti-dependency-cycle): a kind of dependency cycle where some transactions fail to observe each other’s effects. Informally, Snapshot Isolation provides each transaction with an isolated snapshot of the entire database. At commit time, the transaction’s writes are applied atomically to produce a new version of the database. The transaction only commits if no other transaction has written the same keys since the transaction’s snapshot was taken.
 Snapshot Isolation strengthens- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed)by prohibiting G-nonadjacent. It is weaker than- [Serializability](https://antithesis.com#serializability), which prohibits- [G2](https://antithesis.com#g2-anti-dependency-cycle)in general. It is neither stronger nor weaker than- [Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read): Repeatable Read allows some predicate phenomena which Snapshot Isolation doesn’t, and Snapshot Isolation allows some single-item phenomena, like- [Write Skew](https://antithesis.com#a5b-write-skew), which Repeatable Read doesn’t.
- [Strong consistency](https://antithesis.com#strong-consistency)
- There is no one accepted definition of “strong consistency,” and the term is used to cover a broad range of consistency models. It can refer to many consistency models, including [Sequential](https://antithesis.com#sequential-consistency-model),[Linearizable](https://antithesis.com#linearizability),[Serializable](https://antithesis.com#serializability),[Strong Session Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-session-serializable),[Strong Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable), and so on. In general, “strong” and “weak” are relative terms.
- [Strong Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable)
- [Strong Serializable](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/strong-serializable)is one of the strongest transactional consistency models. It strengthens- [Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable)by proscribing- [real-time phenomena](https://antithesis.com#real-time-phenomena): the apparent order of transactions must be consistent with their real-time order. If transaction A commits before transaction B begins, B must appear to execute after A.
 Strong Serializability is also stronger than- [Strong Session Serializability](https://antithesis.com#strong-session-serializable), which allows- [processes](https://antithesis.com#process)to skew relative to one another. If one considers a transaction as a single- [operation](https://antithesis.com#operation), and the database as a single- [object](https://antithesis.com#object), Strong Serializability is equivalent to- [Linearizability](https://antithesis.com#linearizability).
- [Strong Session Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-session-serializable)
- [Strong Session Serializable](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~kmsalem/pubs/DaudjeeICDE04.pdf)is a relatively strong transactional consistency model. It strengthens- [Serializable](https://antithesis.com#serializability)by proscribing session phenomena: the apparent order of transactions must be consistent with the order within each session. If we identify each session as a- [process](https://antithesis.com#process), Strong Session Serializable requires that the graph of- [write-write](https://antithesis.com#write-write-dependency),- [write-read](https://antithesis.com#write-read-dependency),- [read-write](https://antithesis.com#read-write-dependency), and- [session dependencies](https://antithesis.com#session-dependency)between transactions is acyclic.
 Strong Session Serializable is weaker than- [Strong Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable), which ensures that all transactions, regardless of which process performs them, appear to execute in real-time order.
- [Strong Session Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#strong-session-snapshot-isolation)
- [Strong Session Snapshot Isolation](https://www.vldb.org/conf/2006/p715-daudjee.pdf)is a relatively strong transactional consistency model. Just as- [Strong Session Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-session-serializable)strengthens- [Serializable](https://antithesis.com#serializability), Strong Session Snapshot Isolation strengthens- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation)by proscribing session phenomena: the apparent order of transactions must be consistent with the order within each session. If we identify each session as a- [process](https://antithesis.com#process), Strong Session Snapshot Isolation requires that the graph of- [write-write](https://antithesis.com#write-write-dependency),- [write-read](https://antithesis.com#write-read-dependency),- [read-write](https://antithesis.com#read-write-dependency), and- [session dependencies](https://antithesis.com#session-dependency)has no cycles, except for cycles which have adjacent read-write edges.
 Strong Session Snapshot Isolation is weaker than- [Strong Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#strong-snapshot-isolation), which enforces real-time order between processes, not just within each process.
- [Strong Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#strong-snapshot-isolation)
- [Strong Snapshot Isolation](https://www.vldb.org/conf/2006/p715-daudjee.pdf)is a relatively strong transactional consistency model. Just as- [Strong Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable)strengthens- [Serializable](https://antithesis.com#serializability), Strong Snapshot Isolation strengthens- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation)by proscribing- [real-time phenomena](https://antithesis.com#real-time-phenomena): the apparent order of transactions must be consistent with their real-time order. If transaction A commits before transaction B begins, B’s snapshot must reflect A’s commit. Strong Snapshot Isolation requires that the graph of- [write-write](https://antithesis.com#write-write-dependency),- [write-read](https://antithesis.com#write-read-dependency),- [read-write](https://antithesis.com#read-write-dependency), and- [real-time dependencies](https://antithesis.com#real-time-dependency)is acyclic, except for cycles which have adjacent read-write edges.
 Strong Snapshot Isolation is also stronger than- [Strong Session Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#strong-session-snapshot-isolation), which only enforces order within each- [process](https://antithesis.com#process), rather than across all processes.
- [Writes Follow Reads](https://antithesis.com#writes-follow-reads)
- Writes Follow Reads is a consistency model which ensures that if a [process](https://antithesis.com#process)performs a read R observing some write W1, any later write W2 that process executes must take effect after W1. Reading a value “seals” the past.

These are different ways systems can be available.

| Model | Operations succeed when… | Achievable consistency models |
|---|---|---|
| Total | The node is non-faulty | [Monotonic Atomic View](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-atomic-view),[Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed),[Read Uncommitted](https://antithesis.com#read-uncommitted),[Monotonic Read](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-reads),[Monotonic Write](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-writes),[Writes Follow Reads](https://antithesis.com#writes-follow-reads) |
| Sticky | A non-faulty client is connected to a non-faulty server | [Causal](https://antithesis.com#causal-consistency),[Read Your Writes](https://antithesis.com#read-your-writes) |
| Majority | The node is non-faulty and can communicate with a majority of nodes | [Sequential](https://antithesis.com#sequential-consistency-model),[Linearizable](https://antithesis.com#linearizability),[Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation),[Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read),[Serializable](https://antithesis.com#serializability),[Strong Serializable](https://antithesis.com#strong-serializable) |

- [High availability](https://antithesis.com#high-availability)
- Many systems claim to offer high availability, but [the term is not well-defined](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2015/05/11/please-stop-calling-databases-cp-or-ap.html). The[Megastore paper](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2011/Papers/CIDR11_Paper32.pdf)uses “high availability” to mean majority availability, but the[Dynamo paper](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)uses the term to mean total availability.
 One working definition is that a highly available system is available much of the time; this is the definition adopted in, for example,[Ladin, Liskov, Shrira, and Ghemawat’s “Providing High Availability Using Lazy Replication.”](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spr24/cos418/papers/lazy.pdf)Another definition is that a highly available system should generally be available more often than a single node.
- [Total availability](https://antithesis.com#total-availability)
- [Totally available](https://dataintensive.net/)systems ensure that every non-faulty node can execute any- [operation](https://antithesis.com#operation). Operations continue to execute even when other nodes, or the network between them, fail.
 Total availability is particularly useful for mobile apps, geo-replicated systems, and IOT devices with limited power or connectivity. Total availability also has important performance implications. Regardless of node or network failures, a totally available system can process requests without waiting for any network communication. This is particularly useful for latency-sensitive applications.
 - [Consistency models](https://antithesis.com#consistency-models)like- [Read Uncommitted](https://antithesis.com#read-uncommitted),- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed),- [Monotonic Atomic View](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-atomic-view),- [Writes Follow Reads](https://antithesis.com#writes-follow-reads),- [Monotonic Reads](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-reads), and- [Monotonic Writes](https://antithesis.com#monotonic-writes)can all be implemented in totally available systems.
 - [Bailis et al](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol7/p181-bailis.pdf),- [Abadi](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf), and- [DeCandia et al’s Dynamo paper](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)all call this model of availability “highly available.” Gilbert & Lynch simply call it “available” in- [their CAP Theorem paper](https://users.ece.cmu.edu/~adrian/731-sp04/readings/GL-cap.pdf), as do the- [PNUTS](https://sites.cs.ucsb.edu/~agrawal/fall2009/PNUTS.pdf)and- [COPS papers](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~dga/papers/cops-sosp2011.pdf). We call it “total availability,” in an attempt to disambiguate.
- [Majority availability](https://antithesis.com#majority-availability)
- Majority available systems ensure that if a majority of non-faulty nodes can communicate with one another, those nodes can execute [operations](https://antithesis.com#operation). Operations may fail on faulty nodes, or when nodes cannot exchange messages with a majority. Many systems use “just over half” as their majority, but some[Byzantine-fault](https://antithesis.com#byzantine-fault)-tolerant systems use a different fraction, like a two-thirds majority. Some systems can use large quorums for (e.g.) leader election[in exchange for](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1608.06696)smaller quorums when committing operations using a stable leader.
 Consistency models like[Sequential](https://antithesis.com#sequential-consistency-model),[Linearizable](https://antithesis.com#linearizability),[Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation),[Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read),[Serializable](https://antithesis.com#serializability), and their stronger variants[can only be, at best, majority available](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models). In practice, systems like Zookeeper, Raft, Consul, MongoDB, and CockroachDB are (broadly speaking) majority available.
 The distributed systems literature uses varying names for this model.[Bailis et al’s HAT paper](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol7/p181-bailis.pdf)calls it “unavailable,” whereas[Megastore](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2011/Papers/CIDR11_Paper32.pdf)calls it “highly available.” We opt for “majority available.”
- [Sticky availability](https://antithesis.com#sticky-availability)
- [Sticky availability](http://www.bailis.org/papers/hat-vldb2014.pdf)means that if a client executes an operation against a database state that reflects all the client’s past transactions, it eventually receives a response – even in the presence of indefinite node or network failures. Broadly speaking, stateless clients must “stick” to one server, which ensures the consistency of that client’s- [operations](https://antithesis.com#operation). In the limiting case where every process is a server (or maintains its own state) this reduces to total availability.
 Consistency models like- [Read Your Writes](https://antithesis.com#read-your-writes)and- [Causal consistency](https://antithesis.com#causal-consistency)can be implemented in sticky available systems, or in- [totally available](https://antithesis.com#total-availability)systems in which all processes retain state about the past.

A phenomenon is something a system does which someone, somewhere, thought was a bad idea. For example, [G0 (Write Cycle)](https://antithesis.com#g0-write-cycle) describes a set of transactions which all overwrite each other. Since some names for phenomena have multiple interpretations, we try to use the less-ambiguous, short names presented in the literature – e.g. [G1a](https://antithesis.com#g1a-aborted-read) for “aborted read.”

- [A5A (Read Skew)](https://antithesis.com#a5a-read-skew)
- [A5A (also known as Read Skew)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/a5a)is a phenomenon where a transaction observes part, but not all, of another transaction’s writes. A5A is a special case of- [G-single](https://antithesis.com#g-single-single-anti-dependency-cycle). It is allowed by- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed), but forbidden by- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation)and- [Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read).
- [A5B (Write Skew)](https://antithesis.com#a5b-write-skew)
- [A5B (also known as Write Skew)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/a5b)is a phenomenon where two transactions write different objects, and each fails to observe the other’s write. A5B is a special case of- [G2-item](https://antithesis.com#g2-item-item-anti-dependency-cycle); it is allowed by- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation), but is forbidden by- [Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read).
- [Fractured Read](https://antithesis.com#fractured-read)
- [Fractured Read](http://www.bailis.org/papers/ramp-sigmod2014.pdf)is a phenomenon where one transaction writes two- [objects](https://antithesis.com#object)x and y, and a second transaction reads that version of x, but an older version of y. Fractured Reads are prevented by- [Read Atomic](https://antithesis.com#read-atomic).
- [G0 (Write Cycle)](https://antithesis.com#g0-write-cycle)
- [G0 (also known as Write Cycle)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/g0)is a phenomenon where a set of transactions overwrite one another, forming a cycle linked purely by- [write-write dependencies](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies). G0 is proscribed by- [Read Uncommitted](https://antithesis.com#read-uncommitted).
- [G1](https://antithesis.com#g1)
- G1 is the conjunction of three phenomena: [G1a (Aborted Read)](https://antithesis.com#g1a-aborted-read),[G1b (Intermediate Read)](https://antithesis.com#g1b-intermediate-read), and[G1c (Cyclic Information Flow)](https://antithesis.com#g1c-cyclic-information-flow). G1 is used to define[Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed).
- [G1a (Aborted Read)](https://antithesis.com#g1a-aborted-read)
- [G1a (also known as Aborted Read)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/g1a)is a phenomenon where an aborted transaction’s write is visible to a committed transaction. G1a is prohibited by- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed).
 Checking for G1a is straightforward: one builds a set of the- [versions](https://antithesis.com#version)written by every aborted transaction, then scans every committed read. If any sees an aborted transaction, one has a direct example of G1a.
- [G1b (Intermediate Read)](https://antithesis.com#g1b-intermediate-read)
- [G1b (also known as Intermediate Read)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/g1b)is a phenomenon where a transaction reads a version of some- [object](https://antithesis.com#object)from the middle of a different transaction; i.e., a version other than that transaction’s last write of that object. G1b is prohibited by- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed).
 Checking for G1b is straightforward. Start by scanning through every transaction, building up a set of intermediate- [versions](https://antithesis.com#version): those versions which were overwritten by writes later in the same transaction. Then scan every committed read: if any observes an intermediate version, it constitutes an example of G1b.
- [G1c (Cyclic Information Flow)](https://antithesis.com#g1c-cyclic-information-flow)
- [G1c (also known as Cyclic Information Flow)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/g1c)is a phenomenon where a set of transactions all observe or overwrite each other’s writes. G1c is prohibited by- [Read Committed](https://antithesis.com#read-committed).
- [Garbage Read](https://antithesis.com#garbage-read)
- Garbage Read is a phenomenon where a database returns a version of some object that was not the product of any write(s). Garbage reads can occur due to memory corruption, serialization errors, race conditions, and more. We are not aware of a formal name for this phenomenon, but it occurs in a surprising number of real systems.
 Checking for garbage reads is relatively simple.
- [G-single (Single Anti-Dependency Cycle)](https://antithesis.com#g-single-single-anti-dependency-cycle)
- [G-single (also known as Single Anti-dependency Cycle)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/g-single)is a phenomenon where a set of transactions are linked in a cycle whose edges are- [write-write, write-read, or read-write dependencies](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies), and there is exactly one read-write dependency. This is one of the cycles proscribed by- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation).
- [G-nonadjacent (Non-Adjacent Anti-Dependency Cycle)](https://antithesis.com#g-nonadjacent-non-adjacent-anti-dependency-cycle)
- [G-nonadjacent](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/g-nonadjacent)is a phenomenon where a set of transactions are linked in a cycle whose edges consist of- [write-write, write-read, or read-write dependencies](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies), and no two read-write dependencies appear adjacent to each other. This is not a standardized term in the literature, but it is the general kind of cycle proscribed by- [Snapshot Isolation](https://antithesis.com#snapshot-isolation).
- [G2-item (Item Anti-Dependency Cycle)](https://antithesis.com#g2-item-item-anti-dependency-cycle)
- [G2-item (also known as an Item Anti-Dependency Cycle)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/g2-item)is a phenomenon where a set of transactions are linked in a cycle whose edges consist of- [write-write, write-read, or read-write dependencies](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies)purely on single- [objects](https://antithesis.com#object), rather than predicates. This is the general kind of cycle proscribed by- [Repeatable Read](https://antithesis.com#repeatable-read).
- [G2 (Anti-Dependency Cycle)](https://antithesis.com#g2-anti-dependency-cycle)
- [G2 (also known as an Anti-Dependency Cycle)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/phenomena/g2)is a phenomenon where a set of transactions are linked in a cycle whose edges consist of- [write-write, write-read, or read-write dependencies](https://jepsen.io/consistency/dependencies). These cycles are proscribed by- [Serializability](https://antithesis.com#serializability).
- [Internal Consistency Anomaly](https://antithesis.com#internal-consistency-anomaly)
- An [Internal Consistency Anomaly](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol042-concur2015/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2015.58/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2015.58.pdf)occurs when a transaction fails to provide sequential semantics within a single transaction. For read-write registers, an internal violation occurs when a read of[object](https://antithesis.com#object)x fails to observe that transaction’s most recent write of x, or the version of x from the start of the transaction. This comes from[Cerone, Bernardi, and Gotsman’s A Framework for Transactional Consistency Models with Atomic Visibility](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol042-concur2015/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2015.58/LIPIcs.CONCUR.2015.58.pdf), where it is formalized as the axiom INT. Similar behaviors are required in[Adya’s](https://www.pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/adya-phd.pdf)and[Alvisi et al’s](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.06670)formalisms.
 Internal consistency is relatively easy to verify. Within each transaction independently, one steps through each sub-[operation](https://antithesis.com#operation)and keeps track of what the database state should have been, given that operation. For instance, once one observes a write of x=5, any later reads of x should observe 5, until another write of x supervenes.
- [Long Fork](https://antithesis.com#long-fork)
